1 SUMMARY OF PROJECT BENEFITS
1.1 Unique Project Benefits
Outcome or impact estimated by the end of project lifetime
Section
reference
1) greenhouse gas emissions Reduction
The project is expected to prevent emissions totaling 74,417,068 tCO2e by averting
planned deforestation and forest degradation throughout its crediting period.
2,3
2) Community livelihood improvement and resilience
The project is designed to generate positive impacts on local community livelihoods by
creating sustainable income opportunities and improving access to managed natural
resources. These measures are expected to reduce dependence on practices that lead to
deforestation and forest degradation.
4
3) Biodiversity and ecosystem conservation
The project is expected to yield significant benefits for biodiversity conservation and
ecosystem service enhancement. Key outcomes include the preservation of critical habitats
and increased species richness and diversity across the project zone.
In addition, the project will contribute to the improvement of multiple ecosystem services,
such as enhanced water quality, strengthened soil conservation, regulation of local
microclimates, and sustainable provision of non-timber forest products.
5

1.2 Standardized Benefit Metrics
1 Land with woody vegetation that meets an internationally accepted definition (e.g., UNFCCC, FAO, or IPCC) of what constitutes a forest,
which includes threshold parameters, such as minimum forest area, tree height and level of crown cover, and may include mature,
secondary, degraded and wetland forests (VCS Program Definitions)
2 Reduced emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD) - Activities that reduce GHG emissions by slowing or stopping
conversion of forests to non-forest land and/or reduce the degradation of forest land where forest biomass is lost (VCS Program
Definitions)
3 Afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (ARR) - Activities that increase carbon stocks in woody biomass (and in some cases soils) by
establishing, increasing and/or restoring vegetative cover through the planting, sowing and/or human -assisted natural regeneration of
woody vegetation (VCS Program Definitions)
4 Improved forest management (IFM) - Activities that change forest management practices and increase carbon stock on forest lands
managed for wood products such as saw timber, pulpwood, and fuelwood (VCS Program Definitions)

2 PROJECT DETAILS
2.1 Project Goals, Design and Long-Term Viability
2.1.1 Summary Description of the Project (VCS, 3.2, 3.6, 3.10, 3.11, 3.13, 3.14; CCB, G1.2)
The Grande Sun Gabon Ogooué-Ivindo REDD+ Project is a developed by Hainan Grande Sun
Carbon Energy Technology Co.,LTD, with the objective of promoting forest conservation and the
reduction of potential greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions derived from planned deforestation and
forest degradation. With a focus on forest preservation, the project's primary land use remains
unchanged, barring the reserved area (up to 15% of the total project area) earmarked for future
expansion and development of the existing villages and provision of additional and better social
services (including the respective facilities and access roads whereto) to the local communities.
The project falls under the category of Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest
Degradation (REDD) in the Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector. The project
covers an area of 146,331 hectares and is rich in forest and ecological resources. The Grande
Sun Gabon Ogooué-Ivindo REDD+ Project, situated in the Mvoung, Ivindo, and Zadié
departments of the Ogooué-Ivindo Province, Gabon ("the Project Area").
Locations of the Project Area
The Project Area was previously a planned logging area, yet now it is under the protection of
conservation agreements. The project's primary land use remains unchanged, with a focus on
forest conservation, and it also provides more and better social services (including the relevant
facilities and access roads to these facilities) to the local communities.

Page 10
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
10
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
The project follows the CCB standards, generating benefits for the climate, community, and
biodiversity through activities that promote forest cover conservation and local social
development. The project conserves 146,331 hectares of local forests and their biodiversity
through annual monitoring of forest cover and regular monitoring of species. The local
communities will be benefited through actions of social engagement, education, digital
inclusion, health, access to water, employment and income generation, training and
qualification, rural extension, and infrastructure.
Through the above-mentioned project activities, the forests under the Grande Sun Project will
be protected from clearance, and net GHG emission reductions or removals will be achieved. At
the end of the project, with the conservation of the total project area, it is estimated a total
avoided emissions of 74,417,068 tons of Greenhouse Gases (GHG) (CO₂e) (2,976,682.72
tCO₂e/year), contributing to the mitigation of climate change.
The project is not located within a jurisdiction covered by a jurisdictional REDD+ program.

2.1.3 Sectoral Scope and Project Type (VCS, 3.2)
Sectoral scope 14: Agriculture, forestry, and other land use
AFOLU project category 12 Reduced Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation (REDD)
Project activity type Avoiding Planned Deforestation and/or Degradation (APDD)
2.1.4 Project Eligibility (VCS, 3.1, 3.6, 3.8, 3.18, 4.1; CCB Program Rules, 4.2.4, 4.6.4)
According to the VCS Methodology Requirements for REDD+, the project qualifies through its
implementation of activities that effectively reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by mitigating
deforestation. It is therefore eligible for inclusion under both the VCS and the CCB Program.
This project is classified as a REDD+ initiative under the activity type Avoiding Planned
Deforestation and Degradation (APDD), in accordance with Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard
v4.7. The following justifications support this categorization:
12 See Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard

Page 11
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
11
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
a) The project is designed to prevent the planned commercial deforestation of tropical forest for
agricultural and timber expansion.
b) A land-use transition plan is implemented by the project, prioritizing forest conservation,
sustainable community livelihoods, and carbon sequestration, thereby directly replacing the
legally authorized deforestation scenario.
c) The project area is not located within a jurisdiction that is governed by an approved or
operational jurisdictional REDD+ program under the VCS or JNR frameworks.
Therefore, the project meets the eligibility criteria for APDD under the VCS Standard v4.7,
Appendix 1.

3.2.1 There are currently six AFOLU project
categories eligible under the VCS Program, as
defined in Appendix 1 Eligible AFOLU Project
Categories below: afforestation, reforestation
and revegetation (ARR), agricultural land
management (ALM), improved forest
management (IFM), reduced emissions from
deforestation and degradation (REDD),
avoided conversion of grasslands and
shrublands (ACoGS), and wetland restoration
and conservation (WRC). Further specification
with respect to eligible activities which may
be included within methodologies approved
under the VCS Program can be found in the
VCS Methodology Requirements.
This is an eligible AFOLU project category
under the VCS Program: Reduced Emissions
from Deforestation and Degradation (REDD).
This project is categorized as a REDD project
with the activity type of Avoiding Planned
Deforestation and Degradation (APDD), as
defined under Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard
v4.7. The following justifications are provided:
- The project aims to prevent planned
commercial deforestation of tropical forest for
timber development.
- The project implements a land-use transition
plan emphasizing forest conservation,
sustainable livelihoods, and carbon
sequestration, replacing the legal planned
deforestation scenario.
- The project does not take place in a
jurisdiction that is covered by an approved or

that will be impacted by the project activities.

proponent must consider the significance of
user populations and how deeply affected
they may be by the project activities, such
that distant or intermittent user groups who
will be affected in very limited ways by the
project need not be defined as stakeholders.

information on stakeholders at the start of

A1.5 Eligible REDD activities are those that
reduce net GHG emissions by reducing
deforestation and/or degradation of forests.
Deforestation is the direct, human-induced
conversion of forest land to non-forest land.
Degradation is the persistent reduction of
canopy cover and/or carbon stocks in a forest
due to human activities such as animal
grazing, fuelwood extraction, timber removal
or other such activities, but which does not
result in the conversion of forest to non-forest
land (which would be classified as
deforestation), and qualifies as forests
remaining as forests, such as set out under
the IPCC 2003 Good Practice Guidance. The
project area shall meet an internationally
accepted definition of forest, such as those
based on UNFCCC host-country thresholds or
FAO definitions, and shall qualify as forest for
a minimum of 10 years before the project
start date. The definition of forest may
include mature forests, secondary forests,
and degraded forests. Under the VCS
Program, secondary forests are considered to
be forests that have been cleared and have
recovered naturally and that are at least 10
years old and meet the lower bound of the
forest threshold parameters at the start of the
project. Forested wetlands, such as floodplain
forests, peatland forests and mangrove
forests, are also eligible provided they meet
the forest definition requirements mentioned
above.
The GIS pictures will be provided in the formal
version.
A1.6 Activities covered under the REDD
project category are those that are designed
to stop planned (designated and sanctioned)
deforestation or unplanned (unsanctioned)
deforestation and/or degradation. Avoided
planned degradation is classified as IFM.
The project activity is designed to stop
planned (sanctioned) deforestation as
described throughout the project description.
A1.7 Activities that stop unsanctioned
deforestation and/or illegal degradation (such
as removal of fuelwood or timber extracted by
non-concessionaires) on lands that are legally
sanctioned for timber production are eligible
as REDD activities. However, activities that
reduce or stop logging only, followed by
protection, on forest lands legally designated
or sanctioned for forestry activities are
included within IFM. Projects that include
both avoided unplanned deforestation and/or
degradation as well as stopping sanctioned
logging activities, shall follow the REDD
guidelines for the unplanned deforestation
and/or degradation and the IFM guidelines
In case future project activity instances have
areas legally sanctioned for timber production,
baseline and project activity shall comprehend
unsanctioned deforestation and/or illegal
degradation, not the reduction of logging.

CCB & VCS Project Description

20
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
for the sanctioned logging activities, and shall
follow the requirements set out in Section
3.6.2
A1.8 Eligible REDD activities include:
1) Avoiding Planned Deforestation (APD):
This category includes activities that
reduce net GHG emissions by
permanently stopping or reducing
deforestation on forest lands that are
legally authorized and documented for
conversion. Planned deforestation
encompasses activities where a forest
system would have been cleared and
replaced by a different forest system with
a lower carbon stock and where the
recovery of timber was not the primary
objective of the initial forest clearance
2) Avoiding Unplanned Deforestation and/or
Degradation (AUDD): This category
includes activities that reduce net GHG
emissions by stopping deforestation
and/or degradation of degraded to
mature forests that would have occurred
in any forest configuration.
The present Project Activity is within category
Avoiding Planned Deforestation and/or
Degradation (APDD).
This project is categorized as a REDD project
with the activity type of Avoiding Planned
Deforestation and Degradation (APDD), as
defined under Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard
v4.7. The following justifications are provided:
- The project aims to prevent planned
commercial deforestation of tropical forest for
agricultural and timber development.
- The project implements a land-use transition
plan emphasizing forest conservation,
sustainable livelihoods, and carbon
sequestration, replacing the legal planned
deforestation scenario.
- The project does not take place in a
jurisdiction that is covered by an approved or
operational jurisdictional REDD+ program
under the VCS or JNR frameworks.
Therefore, the project meets the eligibility
criteria for APDD under the VCS Standard
v4.7, Appendix 1.

2.1.9 Project Ownership (VCS, 3.2, 3.7, 3.10; CCB, G5.8)
The Grande Sun Project comprises five plots located in the province of Ogooué-Ivindo. Three
plots, totaling 40,584 hectares, are situated in Mvoung. The remaining two plots are located in
Ivindo and Zadié, covering 24,514 hectares and 81,233 hectares, respectively. The total area of
the project amounts to 146,331 hectares.
The land ownership of these five plots belongs to the state, namely Gabon. However, ENB has
acquired the forest concession rights (PFA - Permis Forestier Associé) for the three plots in
Mvoung (Concession Numbers: 38/04, 94/04, 98/04), an industrial exploitation permit (PI -
Permis Industriel) for the plot in Ivindo (Permit Number: 15/02), and an industrial exploitation
permit (PI - Permis Industriel) for the plot in Zadié(Permit Number: 16/02).
ENB has further established the legality of industrial development, exploitation, and processing
of forest resources within these five concession areas by signing the Provisional Convention on
Development, Exploitation, and Transformation (CPAET) with the Gabonese Water and Forest
Administration of Gabon.

2.1.10 Project Start Date (VCS, 3.8)
Project start date 15-October-2022
Justification In the absence of the REDD project, this area would have undergone
logging in accordance with the management plan submitted to the
government for approval, thus leading to deforestation in the region.
The project start date is October 15, 2022, which is the date when
ENB decided to suspend the forest development plan and switch to
developing the REDD project. From that date, ENB internally initiated
the CCB-and-VCS application project, held a project launch meeting,
and carried out a series of preparatory activities, such as mobilizing
internal departments to participate and initiating external actions like
contacting the local government to submit a new management plan
and liaising with local communities to inform them about the project.
According to the VCS Program, the start date of an Agriculture,
Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU) project corresponds to the
moment when actions resulting in GHG emission reductions or
removals are initiated. In the Grande Sun REDD+ project, this
includes the decision by ENB, the owner of the forest development
rights, to halt the planned timber development and conserve the area.
Additional early-stage activities include specific stakeholder
engagement and the implementation of social and environmental
safeguards, as detailed in section 2.1.19.

2.1.14 Physical Parameters (CCB, G1.3)
The project area encompasses a total of 146,331 hectares, comprising five plots located within
the Ogooué-Ivindo Province, specifically in the departments of Ivindo, Mvoung, and Zadié.
These include one plot in Makokou (Ivindo Department) covering 24,514 hectares; one plot in
Mékambo (ZadiéDepartment) covering 81,233 hectares; and three plots in Ovan (Mvoung
Department) with a combined area of 40,584 hectares.
Climate
The project area, located in Ogooué-Ivindo Province (specifically Ovan, Makokou, and
Mékambo), exhibits a characteristic pure equatorial climate. This climate is defined by two
distinct rainy seasons (September-December and March-June) interspersed with two dry
seasons of similar intensity. The wettest months are September-October (first rainy season) and
March-April (second rainy season), with the eastern region (Mékambo) receiving higher
precipitation than the western zone.

Page 25
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
25
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Critical climatic data includes an average annual rainfall of 1,680.6 mm and an average annual
temperature of 23.8°C. Extreme records show significant variability: maximum rainfall reaches
2,379 mm while minimum rainfall drops to 787.2 mm, and temperatures range from a high of
35.5°C to a low of 13°C. This climatic profile confirms high humidity with marked seasonal
precipitation patterns and moderate thermal stability typical of equatorial regions, while also
indicating considerable interannual variability in rainfall intensity.

Topography, Soil, and Hydrology
The project are is located in the Ogooué-Ivindo Province, with over two-thirds of its area situated
in the eastern Mékambo region and the remainder in the more western Makokou and Ovan
regions. This area is part of the northern geological massif of Gabon, comparable to the Chaillu
massif. Its eastern portion contains significant iron deposits associated with itabirites
(Mékambo, Makokou, Ovan, Mitzic, Bélinga, Minvoul). The region encompasses crystalline and
crystallophyllian facies. Pegmatites are associated with these two facies groups, and
additionally, basic and ultra-basic intrusions cross-cut these formations.
The soils in the project area are primarily typical ferralitic soils and deep kaolinitic clays. In the
northeastern zone of Gabon (Bélinga, Batouala, Boka-Boka, Minkébé, Ovan, Mitzic, and
Minvoul) at approximately 1000 meters altitude, itabirites have undergone pedological
processes to form erosion-resistant summit iron crusts.

Page 27
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
27
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
The easternmost part of the project area near Mékambo is situated on a crystalline basement.
This geological unit mainly involves the extension of the Minkébéfoothills within the region and
extends further eastward to the neighboring Congo.
Shallow soils are distributed on surfaces rejuvenated by erosion, featuring steep slopes, low
altitude, and highly fragmented terrain. These soils are generally yellow and clayey, involving
kaolinite. Their very fine structure ensures good permeability, but they are also quite fragile.
Although soil conditions are not entirely uniform across the whole project area, it is important to
note that in the more southern Makokou region, under the influence of the Ivindo River basin,
the geological formations consist of schists, micaschists, quartzites, sedimentary-volcanic
formations, and gneiss typical of eastern Gabon.
Within the project area, the hydrological regime is strongly influenced by the equatorial climate
type, characterized by two maxima and two minima. The two minima are homogeneous in value
and are centered on the months of July and August, respectively. The study area exhibits a
typical pure equatorial climate, with the Makokou region irrigated by the Ivindo River and the
Mékambo region by the ZadiéRiver. The hydrological regimes are also influenced by other
important factors, namely: topography, soil, and vegetation.

Vegetation
The project area exhibits distinct vegetation patterns across its two main regions. The Makokou
zone features a less-exploited forest with lower rainfall, characterized by significant populations
of Okoumé(Aucoumea klaineana) alongside species such as Ozouga (Sacoglottis gabonensis),
Oken (Swartzia fistuloides), Angoa (Erismadelphus exsul), and Ozigo (Dacryodes buttneri). In
contrast, the Mékambo zone represents the transition into an ancient forest belt extending
from the Crystal Mountains to the Chaillu Massif. While floristically related to coastal basin
forests, this area shows notably reduced densities of Okouméand Ozigo. Its vegetation is
distinctly marked by patchy distributions of Caesalpiniaceae species (particularly Andoung of
the genus Monoarthanthus), with better representation of Mimosaceae and Papilionaceae
families compared to the reduced presence of Burseraceae, Irvingiaceae, and Acaciaceae.
The woody diversity within the project area has led to a forest stratification identifying six main
forest types: Cultivated land (CCS), Fallow land (JA), Swamp forest (FM), Degraded forest (DF),
Marantaceae forest (FMA), and Dense forest (DF). The description of each forest stratum is as
follows:
Cultivated land (CCS): Recent crop zones (e.g., cassava, banana, sugarcane) containing
residual stumps of valuable tree species (Moabi, Padouk, Dibétou, Dacryodes, etc.).
Fallow land (JA): Old cultivated areas with colonizing species and remaining timber trees or
stumps from past logging, including Azobé, Dibétou, Tali, Essia, and Okoumé.

Page 30
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
30
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Swamp forest (FM): Floodable area with sparse undergrowth, rich in high-value timber species
such as Azobé, Moabi, Ouka, Pau Rosa, and Bossé.
Degraded forest (DF): Forest formations with low timber density but containing species such as
Iroko, Andoung, Sapelli, Kosipo, Faro, Dibétou, and Okoumé.
Marantaceae forest (FMA): Often rich forest composed of grassy undergrowth (e.g.,
Marantaceae species) and containing timber species such as Andoung, Dossié, Doussié,
Mahogany (Acajou), Limba, and Tali.
Dense forest (DF): Forest containing considerable and exploitable timber volumes, often
remarkable for high-value species such as Wengé, Tali, Tiama, Tchitola, Padouk, Ozigo, Olo,
Iroko, Igaganga, Afo, and Andoung.

2.1.15 Social Parameters (VCS, 3.18; CCB, G1.3)
The project area encompasses a total of 146,331 hectares, comprising five plots located within
the Ogooué-Ivindo Province, specifically in the departments of Ivindo, Mvoung, and Zadié.
These include one plot in Makokou (Ivindo Department) covering 24,514 hectares; one plot in
Mékambo (ZadiéDepartment) covering 81,233 hectares; and three plots in Ovan (Mvoung
Department) with a combined area of 40,584 hectares.
Main settlements
Based on the socio-economic survey of the project area provided by Forest Company,
settlements in the Ogooué-Ivindo Province are primarily distributed across the two departments
of Ivindo and Zadié, with significant concentrations in the Makokou area (predominantly
inhabited by the Fang ethnic group) and the Mékambo area (predominantly inhabited by the
Kota ethnic group). These settlements are distributed along the boundaries of the forest
concession and are predominantly riverside villages. A key characteristic of these main
settlements is their multi-ethnic composition; within a single village, it is common to find a mix
of ethnic groups including the Fang, Kota, Tsogho, Kouélé, Mouéta, Mahongwè, and Koya.
Relevant Historic Conditions

Page 33
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
33
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
The Fang and Kota ethnic groups are currently the majority populations within the project area.
Information regarding population origins is interconnected and difficult to confirm; however,
based on verified sources and accounts from local residents, the following origins can be
stated. The Fang ethnic groups initially migrated from Cameroon to the area, with the first
villages established by the Essenessele and Essensia clans. Recently, an Essanji/Essangui clan
migrated into the Fang community from Equatorial Guinea via Medouneu. Their migration is the
result of tribal group mobility.
The Kota and other ethnic groups (such as Mahongwe, Bagoum, Bakota, and Sake) are
distributed in Zadie Departments. Most of them returned from Congo via routes including along
the ZadiéRiver or crossing the LowéRiver.
It must be noted that, due to the demographic diversity within each village, these ethnic groups
do not entirely share the same origins. In fact, within a single village, one can find not only Fang
and Kota people but also many other ethnic groups. The migrations are primarily related to
village expansion and tribal mobility.
The following map illustrates the migration movements of the riverside communities in this
region.
Figure X: Migratory Movements in the Project Area Zone
At 1:200,000 Scale

Page 34
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
34
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Land use, economic activities, and household income
Local people derive their income from diverse sources, yet they remain heavily dependent on
the primary sale of natural resources, including agricultural produce, bushmeat and fishery
products, and non-timber forest products.
• Agricultural Sales: Cassava and plantains/bananas are the main cash crops.
• Bushmeat and Fishery Sales: Hunting and fishing products are significant sources of cash
income. For instance, 70% of harvested porcupines and 60-75% of harvested
antelope/gazelle are sold.
• Non-Timber Forest Product Sales: This includes palm wine, handicrafts (furniture, fish
traps), and raw materials like rattan and raffia. However, such sales primarily serve to meet
basic household subsistence needs, making it difficult to assess their actual economic
return.
The economic activities of the residents are primarily aimed at meeting basic subsistence
needs rather than large-scale commercial profit. The level of income depends more on external
infrastructure conditions, market accessibility, and environmental factors than on production
capacity itself. The trade volume of all their production activities consistently remains lower
than that for self-consumption. Due to poor road conditions, lack of electricity, and other
infrastructure deficiencies, coupled with poor product preservation conditions, household
income is highly unstable and customer availability is scarce.
Regarding the income structure:
• Women are more organized in financial management, have more diverse income sources
(small-scale trade, ago-processing like cassava wine production), and save more than men.
However, they must wait until the harvest season to obtain substantial earnings.
• Men, while capable of earning significant sums from the sale of bushmeat or furniture, do
so only intermittently; this is not a regular occurrence.
Socio-cultural information
The majority of the population in the project area have migrated from other provinces in Gabon.
Many come from nearby towns and regions such as Woleu-Ntem (including Mitzik and Minvoul)
and Moyen-Ogooué(including Lambarénéand Njolé). Others have migrated from closer
provinces, including Ogooué-Lolo and Haut-Ogooué.
Village mergers have also taken place locally. This process concentrated the population and
also significantly boosted the young labor force in settlements. Most of the local permanent
population is young people aged 10-30, with more women than men. These young people make
up the main labor force of the village.

Page 35
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
35
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
The infrastructure challenges across various regions of Gabon are highly similar. Although the
vast majority of settlements and some villages are equipped with clinics, their operation faces
severe difficulties, particularly due to severe shortages in medical supplies—only 1 to 2
replenishments can be conducted annually, and the distributed medicines are limited to basic
drugs such as paracetamol and maleates.
At the same time, villages generally lack adequate health facilities. A few villages have health
posts, but most are dilapidated, lack dedicated staff, and have no medical reserves. For
example, the health post in Ntsenkele village is not a standard clinic but rather a residential
house repurposed for medical use; locals refer to it as a "dispensary."
Basic education faces operational challenges similar to those of the clinics. Although almost all
village settlements have established schools covering the full academic system, they often
suffer from severe shortages of teaching materials, including basic supplies such as chalk,
arithmetic books, and writing boards, while desks and chairs are mostly dilapidated.
Furthermore, teaching capacity is extremely weak. In some schools, only two teachers are
responsible for all instructional duties, making it difficult for them to track student progress
consistently and effectively—particularly for younger students in preparatory classes.
There are clear regional disparities in school infrastructure conditions: a few villages have
school buildings constructed from durable materials and can ensure adequate teacher staffing,
maintaining relatively normal instruction. However, the more remote the area, the more severe
the situation becomes. During the rainy season, poorly constructed school buildings become
unusable—water leakage not only disrupts classes but also poses safety risks to students.

2.1.17 Project Activities and Theory of Change (VCS, 3.6; CCB, G1.8)
The Grande Sun Project encompasses a total area of 1,463,311 hectares, of which up to 15%
(approximately 219,497 hectares) is designated as a community-use buffer zone to mitigate
potential leakage risks. Prior to the project’s initiation, SOCIETE EXPORT NEGOCE DU BOIS
(E.N.B) Limited had secured logging rights for this forest area under a Provisional Convention on
Development, Exploitation, and Transformation (CPAET) signed with the Gabonese Water and
Forest Administration. Originally intended for development, the area is now transitioning into a
zone dedicated to forest conservation and protection.
The Grande Sun Project focuses on implementing conservation strategies to prevent planned
deforestation across the project zone. By avoiding tree removal or clearing, the project ensures
the long-term preservation of forest cover. The project prohibits the conversion of forested
areas to agricultural or industrial use. This ensures the region remains a stable habitat for
native species, supports sustainable development, and enhances community well-being.
The project implements a variety of forest conservation measures, including the establishment
and management of surveillance teams to monitor suspicious activities and prevent
unauthorized intrusion into the project zone. Additional mitigation actions to avoid planned
deforestation will involve strengthened monitoring efforts, mapping of local deforestation

Page 39
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
39
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
drivers, partnerships with academic and research institutions, and the provision of benefits to
surrounding communities. These initiatives aim to reduce deforestation by creating alternative
sources of income, improving education, and offering vocational training. Through the
implementation of these activities, Grande Sun works in partnership with local communities to
protect their forest areas from deforestation.
By aligning with the UNSDGs, the project delivers focused and directed contributions to
sustainable development. The 17 goals provide a comprehensive mechanism for prioritizing key
resources in the project area—including biodiversity, natural capital, financial and human
resources, social assets, and carbon stocks—to systematically improve local socio-
environmental conditions.
Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation
The impact of these measures is anticipated to result in net GHG emission reductions through
the avoidance of planned deforestation and the consequent maintenance and augmentation of
carbon storage.

Through the introduction of health education initiatives and the setup of local medical facilities,

welfare within a forest conservation framework.

2.1.18 Sustainable Development Contributions (VCS, 3.17)
The project supports Gabon’s national priorities in environmental and climate change, gender
equality, governance, social cohesion, human development, and sustainable economic growth.
It delivers environmental, social, governance, and economic benefits aligned with multiple UN
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
By reducing deforestation and degradation, the project protects forest ecosystems and
biodiversity (SDG 15), including habitats for law-protected species such as African forest
elephants and hippopotamus (SDG 15.5). It maintains vital ecosystem services like water
regulation and carbon storage, supporting climate action (SDG 13) and aligning with the
integration of climate measures into policies (SDG 13.2).
Socially, the project helps preserve cultural traditions tied to forests (SDG 11) and provides
sustainable livelihoods through forest management. Revenue from carbon credits funds
community projects such as schools, clinics, and infrastructure (SDGs 3, 4, 9). Activities like

Page 44
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
44
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
agroforestry offer alternative incomes (SDG 8), while improved access to clean water (SDG 6)
and renewable energy (SDG 7) enhance living conditions.
The project promotes transparency and combats illegal logging through sustainable forest
management (SDG 16). It empowers women, youth, and other stakeholders via inclusive
decision-making (SDGs 5, 10, 16.7), reducing conflict and strengthening governance.
Economically, the project generates revenue for national development, supports job creation in
conservation, and reduces poverty (SDGs 1, 8). It advances Gabon’s goal of sustainable and
inclusive prosperity.
Through REDD+ implementation (SDG 15.2), the project ensures long-term forest and
community sustainability. A dedicated monitoring team will ensure accurate data collection and
reporting. Stakeholders, including government and communities, will receive regular updates
and provide input, ensuring transparency and accountability in tracking progress toward
Gabon’s development goals.

Section not required for the Under Development stage in accordance with Verra's Registration
and Issuance Process v4.7.
2.1.20 Risks to the Project (CCB, G1.10)
Identified
Risk
Potential impact of risk on climate,
community and/or biodiversity benefits
Actions needed and designed to
mitigate the risk
Landslides
and Soil
Erosion
(Natural-
induced)
The risk of landslides and soil erosion in the
area is not widespread but is highly
concentrated in specific vulnerable
environments, primarily steep riverbanks. The
risk is caused by the presence of inherently
fragile terrain, such as steep slopes along
major rivers. The process is catalyzed by the
region's heavy equatorial rainfall, which
rapidly erodes exposed soil and can trigger
slope failures.
The project will implement strict
management rules and maintain
drainage infrastructure (ditches,
culverts) with the objective of
preventing soil erosion, protecting
water quality, and enhancing the
climate resilience of forest
infrastructure.
Disorganized
hunting
(Human-
induced)
Hunting is culturally significant and
fundamental to the way of life of the
indigenous communities residing in the
project area. These activities are presumed to
be conventional and low impact. On the other
hand, hunting activities are conducted in a
disorganized manner without monitoring or
control, and have affected species protected
under the Forest Code, which can be
detrimental to the project's biodiversity goals.
If necessary, ENB will promote fauna
monitoring with an emphasis on
animal species, as well as
environmental education initiatives.

2.1.21 Benefit Permanence (CCB, G1.11)
ENB are facilitating sustainable development across the project area by introducing alternative
cash crops and economic opportunities to stimulate local growth. The project also tries to help
local clans in addressing six priority demands: community projects, infrastructure development
grants, future generation trusts, local savings and loan societies, financial literacy training, and
micro- and small business support.
Through the promotion of sustainable practices and livelihood diversification, the project
reduces high-impact activities such as resource overharvesting, thereby minimizing harm to
biodiversity. These efforts are geared toward empowering communities economically while
promoting habitat conservation.
To sustain and enhance biodiversity outcomes, the project emphasizes community involvement
by collaborating with local clans to strengthen local capacity in resource management.
Education and awareness initiatives are also implemented to instil conservation values across
generations, targeting youth, community leaders, and the general public to foster lasting
ecological stewardship.
2.1.22 Financial Sustainability (CCB, G1.12)
Project activities will be financed by the project proponents from the start date through the first
verification. Following that, revenue generated from greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions
will fund programs designed to amplify the project’s climate, community, and biodiversity
benefits. Evidence of the proponents’ financial commitment will be provided to the validation
and verification body.
2.2 Without-project Land Use Scenario and Additionality
2.2.1 Conditions Prior to Project Initiation and Land Use Scenarios without the Project (VCS, 3.13;
CCB, G2.1)
The Grande Sun Project is in Gabon’s Ogooué-Ivindo Province within a tropical rainforest
ecosystem. This environment is marked by high levels of biodiversity, dense vegetation cover,

CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
46
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
and substantial rainfall—all characteristic of the equatorial climate zone. The forest sustains a
wide variety of plant and animal life, including numerous endemic species.
The Grande Sun Project area has long existed as a natural forest, remaining largely undisturbed
by human activity, and retaining its forest cover over time. It currently continues to be
predominantly wooded, providing essential habitat for native biodiversity while playing a key
role in carbon storage and watershed conservation.
The project area exhibits a tropical rainforest climate, characterized by high humidity, stable
temperatures, and substantial annual rainfall—averaging 1,680.6 mm. The region’s terrain is
part of the northern Gabon massif with geological formations including crystalline facies,
associated pegmatites, and intrusions of basic and ultra-basic rocks. In terms of soils, there are
deep ferralitic and kaolinitic soils, shallow stony soils formed on erosion-rejuvenated surfaces,
and notable summit cuirasses (resistant to erosion) that contain exploitable iron ore;
meanwhile, the soils are generally yellow and clayey (dominated by kaolinite) with fine structure
ensuring good permeability but being quite fragile. The hydrology is complex, featuring a dense
network of major rivers and their tributaries, specifically the Ivindo and Zadiérivers. The
vegetation is not uniformly diverse but is overwhelmingly dominated by swamp forest. This
single forest type constitutes 55.67% of the total area, defining the region's primary ecosystem.
Please refer to 2.1.14 section for further details.
Based on the Provisional Convention on Development, Exploitation, and Transformation (CPAET)
signed between ENB and the Gabonese Water and Forest Administration, ENB has obtained the
rights for the industrial development of forest resources within the concession area. ENB is
required to formulate a management plan and carry out related industrial development
activities. Prior to the launch of the Grande Sun project, this forest area was slated for
clearance as part of a scheduled logging operation. The project's mitigation measures to
prevent planned deforestation will be implemented through enhanced local monitoring,
partnerships with educational and research institutions, and providing benefits to neighboring
communities. These efforts aim to minimize deforestation by offering alternative livelihoods,
improved social services and infrastructure, education, and vocational training. For more
details, please refer to Section 3.1.4.
Potential logging exploitation poses a threat to these woods, the biodiversity they contain, and
the local population. The most likely outcome in the absence of the Grande Sun project is
ongoing logging near accessible areas, followed by the expansion of the road system deep into
the interior and upwards of the mountains. As of 2000, 93% of Ganbon land cover was >30%
tree cover. From 2000 to 2020, Gabon experienced a net change of -99 kha (-0.41%) in tree
cover (Global Forest Watch)13.
For present and prior environmental conditions of the project area, please refer to section
2.1.14. For the baseline scenario, please refer to section 3.1.4.

2.2.2 Most-Likely Scenario Justification (CCB, G2.1)
Section not required for the Under Development stage in accordance with Verra's Registration
and Issuance Process v4.7.
2.2.3 Community and Biodiversity Additionality (CCB, G2.2)
At present, no active initiatives are in place to reduce deforestation in the area, owing to limited
governmental and local resources. Although the government of Gabon has implemented
regulations banning the export of roundwood to curb illegal logging and harvesting, industrial
logging continues to expand rapidly and shows a growing trend14. To the best of our knowledge,
there are no other ongoing projects aimed at halting deforestation or promoting sustainable
land management in the region. These factors clearly demonstrate that the proposed project
activity meets the additionality requirement. For more detail on community and biodiversity
without project scenario, please refer to section 4.1 and 5.1.
2.2.4 Benefits to be used as Offsets (CCB, G2.2)

The Grande Sun project does not intend to use any benefits to communities or biodiversity as

2.3 Safeguards and Stakeholder Engagement
2.3.1 Stakeholder Identification (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB G1.5)
The Grande Sun Project’s Stakeholder Engagement Plan defines the strategies and methods for
involving diverse stakeholder groups throughout the project. Its objective is to ensure inclusive
participation and establish transparent communication channels to support information
exchange, collaboration, and continuous feedback.
Key stakeholder groups were identified and categorized, including local and Indigenous
communities, project proponents, government agencies and policymakers, non-governmental
organizations (NGOs), as well as research and academic institutions. A stakeholder analysis
was conducted to assess their interests, level of influence, and potential impact on the project,
enabling the identification of key representatives within each group for targeted engagement.
Following stakeholder mapping, the project team initiated a consultation process using
methods such as meetings, workshops, interviews, surveys, and focus groups. This approach
ensures that all relevant parties have the opportunity to provide input, voice concerns, and help
shape project design and implementation.
Stakeholder engagement is designed as an iterative process, incorporating ongoing monitoring
and feedback mechanisms. As the project evolves, new stakeholders may be identified, and
existing stakeholders’ priorities may shift. Regular communication is maintained to keep all
parties informed of project progress and to address emerging issues in a timely manner.

2.3.3 Stakeholder Access to Project Documents (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB, G3.1)
Throughout project development and implementation, ENB will ensure full transparency by
making all project documentation—including the project description, monitoring reports, and
supporting materials—accessible to all affected and interested stakeholders. Booklets and
flyers will also be distributed to summarize key project information in an easily understandable
format, supporting effective communication.
The project employs the following mechanisms to ensure broad and inclusive information
sharing:
• Printed Documentation: Physical copies of project documents will be available at the offices
of the Community Council and other designated local facilities. Given the limited internet
connectivity and digital access in the local community, this approach ensures that all local
residents and stakeholders can access relevant information. Booklets and flyers will be
distributed during community engagement events and delivered household-to-household to
maximize outreach coverage.
• Oral Communication: Direct oral engagement has been a primary method for interacting
with local communities. The project design was established through stakeholder workshops
and community assemblies using oral communication. During project monitoring phases,
additional meetings and engagement activities will be organized to update communities on
project progress and outcomes.
• Online Publications: Project documentation will also be published on the VCS and CCB
websites to ensure global accessibility.

52
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
2.3.4 Dissemination of Summary Project Documents (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB, G3.1)
All communication channels outlined in Section 2.3.3 will be used to distribute project
summaries. Summaries of project documentation and monitoring reports will be translated into
French and indigenous languages to ensure accessibility and comprehension by community
members. These summaries will be delivered and presented to relevant stakeholders through
engagement activities such as workshops, meetings, and general assembly's once they become
available.
The administration team will proactively coordinate the distribution of printed materials within
local communities and hold regular meetings to keep stakeholders informed about project
progress. Upon completion of the verification process, audited summary documents will also be
published on the VCS and CCB websites. Additional copies will be provided to other interested
stakeholders upon request.
2.3.5 Informational Meetings with Stakeholders (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB, G3.1)
Informational meetings with communities and local stakeholders constitute a fundamental
component of the project’s engagement and consultation strategy. These gatherings provide a
structured platform to communicate project updates, solicit feedback, address concerns, and
facilitate constructive dialogue between project implementers and community members.
In preparation for these meetings, the project team coordinates closely with local
representatives, government agencies, and community leaders to select appropriate dates,
times, and venues. Key considerations include accessibility, alignment with local schedules,
and ensuring broad representation across stakeholder groups.
Publicity efforts are undertaken to ensure that community members and relevant stakeholders
are aware of the meetings and have an opportunity to attend. Meetings for information are
always advertised at least one month before our trip. Besides, the project remains engaged
with communities through a dedicated team of Community Relations Officers (CROs), who
provide ongoing updates via phone calls and messaging applications as new information or
project milestones are achieved.
2.3.6 Risks from the Project and No Net Harm (VCS, 3.18, 3.19)
The project is dedicated to the conservation of pristine forest ecosystems. It refrains from any
planned logging operations, focusing instead on maintaining the existing forest condition and
preventing the introduction of new risks. No additional negative environmental impacts are
anticipated from the project, as its activities do not involve pollutant emissions to air,
wastewater discharge, noise or vibration, waste generation, or the use of hazardous
substances, chemical pesticides, or fertilizers. For the project risk table, please see Appendix 3.
2.3.7 Community Costs, Risks, and Benefits (CCB, G3.2)

Page 53
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
53
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
When meeting with local communities and indigenous people in the project area, ENB gathers
information about costs, risks, and benefits using a simple and interactive community feedback
approach. This approach was meant to figure out how well they understand things and what
their current situation is like, so ENB can get a clearer picture of how to carry out this project.
During these meetings, ENB explained to the community what costs, risks, and benefits mean,
and ENB encouraged them to share any possible effects they thought the carbon credit project
might have. The discussion was led by experts who made sure to talk in a way that everyone
there could easily understand. Therefore, through this two-way conversation, the community
concluded from this comparison and their discussions that their community conservation
efforts will bring them more benefits than logging due to the following main rationale:
• Local communities widely recognize and highly value the forest’s role in conservation and
its positive contributions to climate stability and biodiversity protection.
• Communities have observed that deforestation has resulted in biodiversity loss and
increased vulnerability to natural disasters.
• The national government is supportive on REDD+ projects, but not deforestation activities
such as logging.
2.3.8 Information to Stakeholders on Validation and Verification Process (VCS, 3.18.6, 3.19; CCB,
G3.3)
During community meetings, detailed information was shared with the local community
regarding the validation and verification process, covering its purpose, procedures, and
logistical arrangements. It was clarified that Project Documents aligned with VCS and CCB
standards must be prepared and undergo rigorous validation and verification. Community
members acknowledged that their active support and coordination are vital to the success of
the VCS+CCB audit, which is required for the issuance of carbon credits.
The following key points were also communicated:
Project Design and Implementation: The project’s objectives, anticipated outcomes, and current
monitoring results were presented to maintain full transparency.
• Risks, Costs, and Benefits: A comprehensive overview of potential risks, costs, and benefits
for stakeholders was provided to facilitate informed understanding.
• Benefit Sharing Mechanism: The framework for equitable distribution of project benefits
among stakeholders was described where applicable.
• Ongoing FPIC Process: Updates were given on the Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC)
process to reaffirm respect for community rights and input.

2.3.9 Site Visit Information and Opportunities to Communicate with Auditor (VCS, 3.18.6; CCB,
G3.3)
The local community will receive notification of the anticipated auditor visit at least one month
ahead of time. Upon confirmation of the exact date, the community leader will be promptly
informed via mobile phone and will subsequently relay the information to other villagers. All
relevant stakeholders will simultaneously receive formal written notification by email.
ENB will coordinate all logistical arrangements for the auditor team’s site visit. On the day of
the audit, the auditors will be introduced to the community in a public gathering, during which
the scope and methodology of the audit will be explained. Focus group discussions will be
organized to facilitate structured dialogue. The meetings will include representatives from local
communities, municipal government bodies, and district development authorities. Community
representatives will be present throughout the audit activities to provide direct responses to
auditor inquiries, ensuring transparency and supporting the effective exchange of information.

2.3.11 Continued Consultation and Adaptive Management (VCS, 3.18; CCB, G3.4)
All stakeholders are encouraged to submit comments and input throughout the duration of the
project. Feedback received will be regularly reviewed and evaluated by the relevant committees.
Written responses will be provided to indicate how each input was considered and whether it
led to any adjustments in project management.
Annual monitoring and evaluation meetings will be convened to collect feedback from key
stakeholders. Attendance will be requested from members of the Management Committee and
the Project Development Committee, which include representatives of the project proponents
and local communities. Agenda items will cover project implementation and monitoring, budget
and investment status, priority actions, key updates, summaries of stakeholder feedback, and
proposed management adaptations. Meeting notes and outcomes will be disseminated to
relevant stakeholders following each session for reference and implementation.

2.3.13 Stakeholder Participation in Decision-Making and Implementation (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB,
G3.6)
To ensure meaningful and inclusive participation of all community groups throughout the
project’s lifecycle—from design and implementation to monitoring and evaluation—a culturally
responsive and comprehensive engagement strategy has been established. The following
measures form the core of this approach:
1. Participatory Workshops
• Inclusive Engagement: Workshops are designed to include diverse community segments
such as women, youth, and representatives from various clans, creating a platform for
sharing local knowledge, perceptions, and expectations.
• Cultural Respect: All sessions are organized in a manner that honors local customs and
traditions. Facilitators receive training to promote a respectful and inclusive environment.
• Accessible Communication: Sessions are conducted in local languages to enable full
comprehension and participation. Interpretation services are provided as needed to ensure
clear dialogue.
2. Stakeholder Committees
• Representative Governance: Committees include members from different clans, women,
and youth to incorporate diverse community perspectives into project decision-making.
• Equitable Representation: Following Gabon Government guidelines, the project has secured
formal consent from most community members, which serves as a clear indication of its
wide-ranging support within the community.
• Transparent Operations: Meetings are conducted with transparency, and minutes and key
decisions are shared openly with the community to maintain accountability and build trust.
3. Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC)

Page 56
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
56
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
• Awareness Activities: FPIC awareness initiatives—including community meetings,
informational sessions, and the distribution of educational materials—have been conducted
to ensure all community members are fully informed about the project and its potential
impacts. For further details, refer to Section 2.5.7.
• Consent Requirement: In compliance with Gabon Government guidelines, formal consent
has been obtained from a large majority of community members, demonstrating broad
community support for the project.
• Ongoing Engagement: FPIC is maintained as a continuous process, with regular updates
provided to the community and ongoing opportunities for feedback throughout the project
lifecycle.
4. Monitoring and Evaluation
• Participatory Monitoring: Community members, including women and youth, are actively
involved in data collection, outcome analysis, and identifying areas for improvement.
• Structured Feedback Channels: Accessible feedback mechanisms—such as community
meetings, suggestion boxes, and digital platforms—enable continuous community input.
• Cultural Relevance: All monitoring and evaluation activities are designed to be culturally
appropriate and accessible to ensure meaningful participation.
5. Capacity Building
• Skill Development: Training sessions and workshops are offered to community members,
with emphasis on women and youth, covering project management, leadership, and
relevant technical skills.
• Community Empowerment: These initiatives aim to strengthen local capacity and
encourage active involvement, fostering a strong sense of ownership and commitment to
the project’s success.
Through these measures, the project promotes inclusive and equitable engagement of all
community segments—including women, youth, and diverse clans—in every phase from design
to evaluation. This approach enhances both the fairness and long-term sustainability of the
project.
2.3.14 Anti-Discrimination Assurance (VCS 3.19; CCB, G3.7)
To foster an environment of inclusivity, diversity, and respect, and to prevent all forms of
discrimination and sexual harassment, the following key measures have been implemented:
1. Non-Discrimination and Anti-Harassment Policy:

Page 57
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
57
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
A clear and comprehensive policy has been established that explicitly prohibits discrimination
and sexual harassment on the basis of gender, race, religion, sexual orientation, or other
protected characteristics. This policy is communicated to all project participants and is readily
accessible.
2. Training and Awareness Initiatives:
Regular training sessions and awareness programs are conducted for project staff, consultants,
contractors, and community members. These initiatives focus on understanding and preventing
discrimination and harassment, highlighting their harmful effects, and reinforcing the
importance of a safe and respectful working environment. Guidance on expected conduct and
reporting procedures is also provided.
3. Equal Opportunity and Inclusive Practices:
The project ensures equal opportunities for all individuals, irrespective of gender, race, religion,
sexual orientation, or other attributes. Diversity and inclusion are actively promoted within
project decision-making, employment, and community engagement processes.
4. Grievance Mechanisms
A formal and confidential grievance mechanism has been established, enabling individuals to
report cases of discrimination or harassment without fear of retaliation. Clear reporting—such
as dedicated hotlines, email addresses, and designated staff—are communicated to all
stakeholders.
5. Investigation and Accountability
A well-defined process is in place to ensure reported incidents are investigated promptly,
impartially, and transparently. Appropriate disciplinary actions, including sanctions, are
enforced against those found responsible.
6. Monitoring and Reporting
The effectiveness of anti-discrimination and anti-harassment measures is regularly monitored
and evaluated. Findings are included in project progress reports, with transparency maintained
regarding incident reports, investigations, and corrective actions.
7. Collaboration with Local Communities
Local communities are actively engaged to incorporate their needs, concerns, and perspectives
into project activities. Community representatives participate in project decision-making to help
ensure their rights are respected throughout the project lifecycle.
8. Partnerships and Due Diligence

CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
58
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Due diligence is conducted on all partner organizations, contractors, and consultants to verify
their adherence to policies preventing discrimination and harassment. Partnerships are
prioritized with entities that demonstrate a strong commitment to equity and inclusion.
ENB considers the integration of these measures into the project’s governance framework
essential to building a culture of respect, fairness, and equality. These protocols will be
periodically reviewed and updated to maintain their relevance and effectiveness over the
course of the project.

2.3.16 Accessibility of the Feedback and Grievance Redress Procedure (VCS, 3.19; CCB, G3.8)
To address the requirements for documenting and publicly sharing the feedback and grievance
redress procedure, ENB has outlined the following approach:
1. Publicity and Accessibility
• The grievance procedure will be disseminated through multiple channels to ensure broad
accessibility, including community notice boards, stakeholder meetings, and local media.
• The procedure will be provided in multiple languages to reflect the linguistic diversity of
local communities.
• Printed copies will be available at community centers, project offices, and other accessible
locations to serve stakeholders with limited internet access.
2. Grievance Submission
• Clear and varied submission channels will be established, such as a dedicated hotline,
email address, physical drop boxes, and designated contact personnel.
• Submission forms will be offered in multiple formats—including online forms, printable
PDFs, and disability-accessible versions—to accommodate diverse needs.

Page 59
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
59
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
3. Documentation and Transparency
• All grievances will be systematically recorded, including submission date, nature of the
issue, and supporting documents, while maintaining strict confidentiality of grievant
information.
• Project responses will be thoroughly documented, including timelines, investigative steps,
resolutions, and outcomes, with summaries made publicly available to ensure
transparency.
4. Public Availability of Information
• To ensure transparency, aggregated and anonymized grievance data—including types of
issues and their resolutions—will be publicly shared via community notice boards and
stakeholder meetings.
• Periodic reports summarizing grievance trends, response timelines, and outcomes will be
published and distributed to relevant stakeholders, regulatory authorities, and other
interested parties as applicable.
5. Privacy and Confidentiality
• The privacy and confidentiality of grievant will be strictly maintained through secure
handling and storage of personal information. Access to sensitive data will be restricted to
authorized personnel involved in the redress process.
• Responses to grievances will be communicated to individuals in a manner that upholds
confidentiality while clearly explaining actions taken and results achieved.
The feedback and grievance mechanism are designed to be widely accessible, transparent, and
trustworthy, thereby strengthening stakeholder engagement throughout the project.
2.3.17 Worker Training (VCS, 3.19; CCB, G3.9)
ENB has developed a structured training program for both project employees and community
participants, designed to build local capacity and reduce dependency on external personnel.
The approach includes comprehensive orientation and skill-building sessions aimed at
empowering community members and ensuring the retention of knowledge and operational
continuity, even amid staff changes.
These efforts support sustainable development by fostering local ownership, enhancing self-
reliance, and strengthening long-term engagement among stakeholders.

2.3.18 Community Employment Opportunities (VCS, 3.19.13; CCB, G3.10)
ENB has established a human resources recruitment policy and a compensation and benefits
framework to ensure a fair and transparent selection process for community-based
employment opportunities. A regularly updated staff list is maintained, and the following
measures will be implemented:
1. Fair and Transparent Recruitment and Selection Criteria
Define clear and specific job requirements, qualifications, and necessary skills for each
position, ensuring alignment with actual job responsibilities.

Page 62
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
62
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Establish selection criteria that are objective, measurable, and strictly job-related, avoiding any
elements that could introduce bias or discrimination—particularly against women, vulnerable
groups, or marginalized communities.
2. Standardized Application and Objective Evaluation Process
Implement a standardized application form or online platform to collect essential candidate
information uniformly.
Screen all applications against predefined job-related criteria to identify candidates meeting
the minimum qualifications.
Apply a structured scoring or rating system to objectively assess and compare applicants’
qualifications, skills, and experience.
3. Diverse Evaluation and Structured Interview Framework
Form a diverse evaluation panel with members trained in impartial and unbiased assessment
methods.
Include representatives from varied backgrounds and areas of expertise to reduce individual
bias and incorporate multiple perspectives into decision-making.
Conduct structured interviews and assessments using pre-defined questions and consistent
evaluation criteria to maintain fairness and comparability.
4. Assessment of Job-Related Competencies
Design job-aligned assessment methods—such as practical tasks, simulations, or work
samples—to directly evaluate candidates’ competencies.
Ensure all assessments reflect actual job requirements and responsibilities to maintain
relevance and accuracy.
Provide candidates with clear instructions and evaluation criteria beforehand to ensure
transparency and preparedness.
5. Transparent Selection Process and Feedback Mechanism
Clearly outline the selection process—including timelines, stages, and evaluation standards—to
all applicants at the outset.
Keep candidates informed at each phase of the process, such as application review, interviews,
and assessments.
Offer constructive feedback to unsuccessful candidates to clarify decision rationale and
support their future improvement.
6. Documentation and Record Keeping

Page 63
CCB & VCS Project Description
CCB Version 3.0, VCS Version 4.4
63
CCB v3.0, VCS v4.4
Maintain comprehensive records of the selection process, including applications, evaluation
scores, interview notes, and assessment outcomes.
Securely and confidentially store all records to ensure privacy and compliance with data
protection regulations.
Document the rationale for candidate selection or non-selection based on predefined criteria to
demonstrate procedural transparency and fairness.
7. Regular Review and Improvement
Conduct regular reviews of the selection process to identify potential biases, inconsistencies, or
areas needing improvement.
Collect feedback from both selection panel members and applicants to evaluate the process’s
fairness and effectiveness.
Implement necessary adjustments based on review findings to ensure ongoing improvement
and adherence to equitable practices.
8. Job Evaluation and Salary Standardization
Establish a quantifiable job evaluation system based on factors such as complexity of duties,
skill requirements, working conditions, and scope of responsibility.
Define standardized salary ranges according to evaluation outcomes to ensure consistency and
transparency in remuneration for the same or similar roles.
9. Pay Equity Auditing and Process Transparency
Conduct regular pay equity audits to analyze compensation distribution differences among
various groups (e.g., gender, region) in comparable positions.
Publicly disclose salary determination principles and adjustment mechanisms, ensuring that
compensation decisions are traceable, explainable, and accessible to all employees.
10. Bias Prevention and Complaint Mechanism
Incorporate pay equity principles into management training to improve recognition and
mitigation of unconscious bias.
Establish an anonymous channel for remuneration complaints, allowing employees to request
pay reviews, with designated personnel processing and responding within a defined timeframe.

Workers involved in the Grande Sun project face risks commonly associated with outdoor field
activities. To mitigate these risks and ensure that all personnel are adequately informed and
protected, ENB has established “Occupational Health and Safety Guidelines” and “Personal
Protective Equipment (PPE) Guidelines” to inform workers about potential risks and supply

contributes to a safer work environment and helps reduce occupational hazards and accidents.
ENB also ensures that all distributed PPE meets relevant safety standards, is properly fitted,
and is regularly maintained. In addition, training is provided to workers on the correct use,
maintenance, and storage of PPE to maximize its protective effectiveness.

framework has been established, outlining ethical standards and behavioral expectations for all
project participants, including team members, contractors, suppliers, and partners. These
policies explicitly prohibit corrupt or unethical actions and provide clear guidelines for conduct.
Anti-Corruption Training and Awareness: Regular training sessions and awareness programs are
conducted to educate all stakeholders on preventing corruption and unethical behavior. The
curriculum covers types of corruption, legal implications, reporting channels, and
consequences of violations, fostering a culture of integrity and vigilance.
Transparent Procurement and Vendor Selection: Rigorous procurement processes are applied,
incorporating competitive bidding, predefined evaluation criteria, and due diligence
assessments. All procurement activities—including proposal requests, bid evaluations, and
contract awards—are thoroughly documented to ensure fairness and mitigate risks of favoritism
or collusion.
Whistleblower Mechanism: A confidential and accessible reporting channel allows individuals to
safely report suspected unethical conduct without fear of retaliation. The mechanism

obligations through credit acquisition.

- Registering and controlling sustainable

- Maintaining a national registry for policies,
projects, concessions, rights, and credits;
- Creating tradable and securable sustainable
development credits;
- Establishing financial mechanisms and oversight
institutions to ensure credit reliability and
national consistency;
- Implementing fiscal incentives and monitoring
systems to promote sustainable practices.
An institutional framework led by the National Council
for Sustainable Development and designated
management bodies is established to oversee
execution.
